knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Dual Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal convergence of scenario multipliers for convex nonanticipativity dual coordination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the concave nonanticipativity dual objective on a finite-dimensional multiplier subspace \(W\), and suppose its maximizer set \(W^\star\) is nonempty. For fixed \(\rho>0\), define \(w^{k+1}\) by \(w^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{w\in W}\{D(w)-\frac{1}{2\rho}\lVert w-w^k\rVert^2\}\). Then \((w^k)\) converges to a point of \(W^\star\), \(D(w^k)\to\sup_WD\), and \(\lVert w^{k+1}-w^k\rVert\to0\). Equivalent Douglas–Rachford or augmented-Lagrangian scenario-dual iterations inherit this conclusion when their dual iterates realize the same resolvent map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact proximal ascent on a proper concave scenario dual converges to a dual solution; equivalent splitting realizations share that convergence regime.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is proper, upper semicontinuous, and concave on \(W\).
\(W^\star\ne\varnothing\).
The proximal dual subproblem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^k\to w^\star\in W^\star\) and \(D(w^k)\to\sup_{w\in W}D(w)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Progressive-Hedging Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-scenario convex progressive-hedging convergence with exact proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{s=1}^m X_s\) be finite-dimensional, let each \(f_s:X_s\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(N\subseteq X\) be the linear nonanticipativity subspace. Assume \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in N}\sum_s p_sf_s(x_s)\ne\varnothing\). With \(p_s>0\), fixed \(\rho>0\), exact scenario proximal solves, and a dual initialization in \(N^\perp\), classical progressive hedging generates primal iterates whose consensus residual tends to zero and whose consensus projections converge to a primal solution; its multipliers converge to a compatible dual solution.

All scenario proximal subproblems are solved exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-bound regularity separating qualitative convergence from locally linear behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be the averaged fixed-point operator representing one exact decomposition step, with \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\). The baseline regularity regime requires only averagedness. A metric-error-bound regime holds on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(F\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) for every \(x\in U\). A global error-bound regime uses \(U=H\). Strong convexity, polyhedrality, or metric subregularity may establish this inequality, but the operative condition is the displayed residual bound itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularity is classified by averagedness alone, a local residual error bound, or a global residual error bound; stronger regimes support stronger rates.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(T\) is averaged and \(F\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) defines the local or global error-bound regime.

children.title: Sublinear Rate Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual complexity for averaged fixed-point representations of convex scenario splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha<1\), let \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and generate \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\). For every \(x^\star\in F\), averagedness gives \(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lVert x^i-Tx^i\rVert^2\le\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\lVert x^0-x^\star\rVert^2\). Consequently, obtaining an iterate with fixed-point residual at most \(\varepsilon\) requires at most \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) iterations, since \(\min_{0\le i\le k}\lVert x^i-Tx^i\rVert^2\le\frac{\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x^0,F)^2}{(1-\alpha)(k+1)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged scenario-splitting iterations attain a best fixed-point residual of order one over the square root of the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged.
\(F\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le i\le k}\lVert x^i-Tx^i\rVert=O((k+1)^{-1/2})\), hence the residual complexity is \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence induced by averagedness and a residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged, let \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\le\kappa\lVert x-Tx\rVert\) throughout a neighborhood containing the tail of \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},F)^2\le q^2\operatorname{dist}(x^k,F)^2\), where \(q^2=1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa^2}<1\) whenever the constants make the displayed factor nonnegative; if it is negative, the inequalities force finite termination. Thus the distance to the solution set decreases Q-linearly on that tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged decomposition map with a local residual error bound converges locally Q-linearly in distance to its fixed-point set.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and \(F\ne\varnothing\).
The residual error bound holds along the iteration tail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},F)\le q\operatorname{dist}(x^k,F)\) for some \(q<1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Degradation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of residual regularity permits convergence without any uniform linear rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\ell^2\), define the linear operator \(T\) by \((Tx)_n=(1-1/n)x_n\). Then \(T\) is self-adjoint, positive, nonexpansive, and averaged, with \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\); nevertheless no constant \(q<1\) satisfies \(\lVert Tx\rVert\le q\lVert x\rVert\) for all \(x\). Moreover, the residual error bound fails because for the unit vector \(e_n\), \(\operatorname{dist}(e_n,\operatorname{Fix}T)=1\) while \(\lVert e_n-Te_n\rVert=1/n\). Thus averagedness alone cannot provide a uniform linear rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a residual error bound, even an averaged linear map may converge while admitting no uniform linear contraction factor.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\ell^2\) with its standard norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No uniform \(q<1\) gives \(\lVert T^kx\rVert\le q^k\lVert x\rVert\) for all \(x\in H\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Guarantee Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex local scenario solves do not inherit global convex progressive-hedging guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two identical scenarios with consensus constraint \(x_1=x_2\) and objective \(\frac12\sum_{s=1}^2(x_s^2-1)^2\). The global consensus solutions are \(x_1=x_2=\pm1\), with value zero. Initialize progressive hedging at \(z^0=0\) and \(w_s^0=0\). If \(\rho>4\), then zero is a strict local minimizer of each augmented scenario objective \((x^2-1)^2+\frac{\rho}{2}x^2\). A local subproblem solver returning this minimizer leaves all primal and dual iterates at zero, whose objective value is one. Thus nonconvex local-solve variants need not reach a global solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex progressive-hedging variant using local subproblem solutions can remain at a strict augmented local minimum that is globally suboptimal.
assumptions_latex: Scenario subproblems may return local rather than global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed iterate \(x_1^k=x_2^k=z^k=0\) is feasible but globally suboptimal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for global guarantees when scenario decisions include integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{Z}^m\) be the feasible set of a scenario-based deterministic equivalent with objective \(f\), where \(m>0\). Suppose scenario splitting produces \(x\in F\) with nonanticipativity residual \(r_{\mathrm{NA}}(x)=0\), and each scenario block is locally optimal or stationary under the method's fixed coordination variables. These facts establish consensus and local block conditions only. Unless every relevant mixed-integer scenario subproblem is solved globally and the coordination procedure supplies a valid global lower bound \(L=f(x)\), one cannot conclude that \(x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in F}f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consensus and scenario-level stationarity do not certify global optimality when integer decisions are present; exact subproblem solutions and a matching global bound are additionally required.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer Guarantee Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary and content kind fit the leaf, but no evidence supports the scenario-specific mixed-integer claim. The statement also presents globally solved subproblems plus a matching lower bound as necessary, although other global certificates could establish optimality.

children.title: Mixed Nonconvex-Integer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Guarantee limits arising when nonconvexity and integrality occur together.

assumptions_latex: The deterministic equivalent contains both a nonconvex continuous component and an integer-valued component.
The decomposition output includes only local scenario solutions and a nonanticipativity residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consensus plus local scenario optimality is generally neither a global-optimality certificate nor a computable global optimality-gap certificate for the mixed nonconvex-integer model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint boundary created by nonconvexity and integrality in scenario-splitting convergence claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{Z}^m\) be nonconvex with \(m>0\), and consider \(\min_{x\in F}f(x)\). A scenario-splitting iterate \(\hat x\) satisfying \(r_{\mathrm{NA}}(\hat x)=0\) and local optimality conditions for every scenario block need not minimize \(f\) over \(F\). Nonconvexity permits distinct local minima, while integrality prevents interpolation arguments used in convex consensus analysis. A global claim therefore requires additional machinery, such as globally solved subproblems together with a valid global lower bound matching \(f(\hat x)\), or an exhaustive global certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With simultaneous nonconvexity and integrality, scenario consensus and local block optimality cannot establish global optimality or a global optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Nonconvex-Integer Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the central warning is plausible, but the mixed nonconvex-integer scenario-decomposition assertions require an inspectable source.

children.title: Scenario-Decomposition Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence families for scenario agreement, dual progress, recovered policies, and termination.

children.title: Nonanticipativity Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence measuring disagreement among scenario decisions sharing an information history.

assumptions_latex: Scenarios sharing an information history use copies of the same decision in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Each scenario has a positive probability weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed residual is zero exactly when all scenario copies satisfy nonanticipativity.

notation.meaning: scenario decision copy at an information-history class

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted consensus residual for one information-history equivalence class; aggregate classes by a norm or sum of squares.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty class \(H\) of scenarios sharing one information history, let \(p_s>0\) and define \(p_H=\sum_{s\in H}p_s\) and \(\bar x=p_H^{-1}\sum_{s\in H}p_sx_s\). The weighted nonanticipativity residual is \[r_H=\left(\sum_{s\in H}p_s\lVert x_s-\bar x\rVert^2\right)^{1/2}.\] It is directly computable from the scenario decisions and probabilities, satisfies \(r_H\geq0\), and certifies exact nonanticipativity precisely when \(r_H=0\), equivalently when \(x_s=\bar x\) for every \(s\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted distance of scenario decisions from their common-history average is computable and vanishes exactly when those decisions agree.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Residual Certificates

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Scenario-Dual Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Bound evidence produced by relaxed nonanticipativity coupling.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is a minimization problem with scenario-separable objective and explicit linear nonanticipativity equations.
Each scenario infimum defining the Lagrangian dual value is computed globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every dual-feasible multiplier produces a verifiable lower bound on the primal optimum; equality with a feasible policy value certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian lower-bound certificate for minimization after relaxing linear nonanticipativity coupling.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(v^*=\inf\{\sum_{s=1}^Sp_sf_s(x_s):x\in X,\ Ax=0\}\), where \(X=\prod_{s=1}^SX_s\) and \(Ax=0\) encodes nonanticipativity. For any multiplier \(\lambda\), define \[d(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}\left(\sum_{s=1}^Sp_sf_s(x_s)+\langle\lambda,Ax\rangle\right).\] The infimum separates by scenario according to the block structure of \(A\), and weak duality gives \(d(\lambda)\leq v^*\). Thus globally computed scenario infima and \(\lambda\) certify the lower bound. If feasible \(\hat x\) also satisfies \(f(\hat x)=d(\lambda)\), then \(\hat x\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing nonanticipativity yields separable scenario infima whose sum is a lower bound; equality with a feasible policy value certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Dual Bound Certificates

children.title: Recovered-Policy Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Evidence attached to information-consistent policies recovered from decomposed solutions.

children.title: Recovered-Policy Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Evidence concerning constraint satisfaction by an information-consistent recovered policy.

assumptions_latex: A recovery map produces one decision for every information history from scenario-wise candidate decisions.
All original deterministic-equivalent constraints and variable domains are explicitly evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Passing the displayed domain, nonanticipativity, and constraint checks certifies feasibility of the recovered policy for the original deterministic equivalent.

notation.meaning: information history of scenario s at stage t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct feasibility certificate for a recovered policy in a finite scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\hat x_s=(\hat x_{s,t})_{t=1}^T\) be recovered decisions on a finite scenario tree. A feasibility certificate consists of checkable records showing \(\hat x_s\in X_s\) for every scenario \(s\), satisfaction of every original linking constraint, and \(\hat x_{s,t}=\hat x_{s',t}\) whenever \(h_t(s)=h_t(s')\). If constraints are represented as \(g_{s,j}(\hat x_s)\leq0\) and \(q_{s,k}(\hat x_s)=0\), the record must verify all such inequalities and equalities within the declared arithmetic tolerance. These checks certify that the history-indexed decisions define a feasible policy for the original deterministic equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recovered policy is certified feasible by checking all scenario domains and constraints together with equality of decisions sharing each information history.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovered-Policy Feasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits, but no source is supplied. Moreover, checking equalities and inequalities merely within a numerical tolerance does not by itself certify exact feasibility unless the model or certificate explicitly incorporates validated error bounds or tolerance-expanded constraints.

children.title: Recovered-Policy Quality
children.top_down_role: Evidence concerning objective quality or decision quality of a recovered policy.

assumptions_latex: The recovered policy is feasible for a finite-scenario minimization problem.
A valid lower bound on the same deterministic equivalent is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The difference between the recovered policy value and the certified lower bound is a valid absolute optimality-gap bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori quality certificate for a feasible recovered policy in a minimization model.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*\) be the optimal value of a finite-scenario minimization problem and let \(\hat x\) be a certified feasible recovered policy. Define \(U=f(\hat x)\), and let \(L\) be any certified lower bound satisfying \(L\leq v^*\), such as a scenario-dual bound computed from globally solved relaxed subproblems. Then \[0\leq U-v^*\leq U-L.\] Hence \(G=U-L\) certifies the absolute suboptimality of \(\hat x\). When \(U\neq0\), a declared relative-gap convention may report \(G/\lvert U\rvert\); the absolute certificate remains valid without a scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible recovered policy, its objective value minus a valid lower bound certifies an upper bound on absolute suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovered-Policy Quality

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Recovery Certification Gaps
children.top_down_role: Cases where available decomposition evidence does not fully certify the recovered policy.

assumptions_latex: Scenario-wise candidate decisions are available, but the recovery procedure has not certified every original constraint.
Any reported bound may come from approximate or locally solved scenario subproblems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without certified feasibility and a valid bound for the original model, no rigorous recovered-policy optimality gap follows from consensus or objective estimates alone.

notation.meaning: optimal value of the original minimization problem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure modes separating heuristic recovery diagnostics from rigorous feasibility and quality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\hat x\) be obtained by averaging, rounding, projection, or another scenario-recovery rule. A small nonanticipativity residual does not certify \(\hat x\in F\) when recovery can violate integrality, dynamics, linking constraints, or scenario feasibility. Likewise, a number \(\tilde L\) computed from approximate or merely local scenario minimizers need not satisfy \(\tilde L\leq v^*\). Therefore \(f(\hat x)-\tilde L\) is not a certified optimality gap unless feasibility of \(\hat x\) and validity of \(\tilde L\) for the same original model are independently verified. Numerical tolerances must also be included in both checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small consensus residuals and heuristic bounds leave a certification gap unless recovery feasibility and lower-bound validity are independently verified for the original model.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Certification Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate failure boundary, but its scenario-recovery and approximate-bound claims have no cited evidence and should remain source-blocked.

children.title: Scenario-Parallel Execution
children.top_down_role: Concurrent solution of scenario or scenario-bundle subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Parallel Execution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous parallel execution of conditionally separable scenario subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\geq 1\) be the number of scenario subproblems, let \(z^k\) be the coordination state at iteration \(k\), let \(\mathcal{S}_s\) be the solution operator for scenario \(s\), and let \(\mathcal{C}\) be the coordination map. Iteration \(k\) concurrently evaluates \(x_s^{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_s(z^k)\) for \(s=1,\ldots,S\), waits for the required results, and sets \(z^{k+1}=\mathcal{C}(x_1^{k+1},\ldots,x_S^{k+1})\). It stops when its declared residual tests pass or returns the last iterate at the iteration limit. If \(P\geq1\) workers receive a disjoint assignment \(\{B_w\}_{w=1}^P\) of the scenarios and \(T_s\geq0\) is the solve time for scenario \(s\), the ideal synchronous solve-phase latency is \[T_{\mathrm{ideal}}=\max_{1\leq w\leq P}\sum_{s\in B_w}T_s.\] Dispatch, communication, synchronization, and coordination costs are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once coordination data are fixed, independent scenario solves can run concurrently; with a declared worker assignment, ideal synchronous solve latency is the largest worker load before overhead.
assumptions_latex: At each coordination iteration, scenario or bundle subproblems are conditionally independent once shared coordination data are fixed.
Enough workers and communication facilities exist to dispatch independent subproblems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scenario solve phase can execute concurrently; its ideal synchronous latency is the largest assigned worker load plus excluded coordination overhead.

children.title: Scenario Grouping Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Grouping strategies balancing coupling retention and parallel granularity.

children.title: Scenario Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Division of the scenario collection into computational partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic partition used to assign scenarios to bundles or workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=\{1,\ldots,S\}\) be a finite scenario index set. A scenario partition into \(G\) groups is an indexed family \(\mathcal{P}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_G\}\) satisfying \(B_g\subseteq\Omega\), \(B_g\neq\varnothing\) for every \(g\), \(B_g\cap B_h=\varnothing\) whenever \(g\neq h\), and \(\bigcup_{g=1}^G B_g=\Omega\). Equivalently, each scenario belongs to exactly one group. A partition is fixed when \(\mathcal{P}\) is unchanged across coordination iterations and dynamic when a declared reassignment rule may replace it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario partitioning assigns every scenario to exactly one nonempty, disjoint group, either permanently or under a declared dynamic reassignment rule.
assumptions_latex: The scenario index set is finite.
Every scenario must be assigned to exactly one group.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A scenario partition is a collection of nonempty, pairwise-disjoint groups whose union is the full scenario set.

children.title: Scenario Bunching
children.top_down_role: Formation of scenario groups that retain selected coupling structure.

assumptions_latex: A finite scenario partition is given.
The grouped subproblem retains each member scenario's objective, constraints, and probability weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scenario bunching replaces separate solves within each group by one joint group solve without deleting the member scenarios from the modeled objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact grouping representation before any optional approximation or scenario reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(\{B_1,ldots,B_G\}\) of the scenario set, scenario bunching associates one grouped subproblem with each \(B_g\). Its objective contribution is \[F_g(x_{B_g})=\sum_{s\in B_g}p_sf_s(x_s),\] and its feasible set retains all scenario constraints for \(s\in B_g\), together with whatever within-group coupling the decomposition specifies. The full objective remains \(\sum_{g=1}^GF_g(x_{B_g})=\sum_{s=1}^Sp_sf_s(x_s)\). Thus bunching changes the computational unit from one scenario to one group; it is not scenario reduction unless objectives or constraints are additionally approximated or discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario bunching jointly solves each partition group while retaining every member scenario's weighted objective and constraints; grouping alone is not scenario reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Bunching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is suitable, but no evidence is supplied for the specific meaning of scenario bunching. The grouped variable \(x_{B_g}\) is also used without an explicit definition.

children.title: Grouping Granularity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance between retained coupling, local workload, and parallel granularity.

assumptions_latex: Scenario solve times and memory demands are nonnegative.
Each group is assigned as one indivisible computational task to a worker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coarser groups reduce task count but can increase critical-path work and per-task memory; finer groups have the opposite structural effects.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural work, memory, and parallelism effects of changing scenario-group size.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(\mathcal{P}=\{B_g\}_{g=1}^G\), define additive estimates \(W(B_g)=\sum_{s\in B_g}W_s\) and \(M(B_g)=\sum_{s\in B_g}M_s\). Merging groups decreases \(G\) and cannot decrease \(\max_gW(B_g)\) or \(\max_gM(B_g)\) under these estimates; splitting groups increases available task parallelism and cannot increase either maximum. Conversely, finer grouping can increase dispatch, synchronization, and coordination traffic because more tasks and boundary quantities are exposed. These are structural tradeoffs, not a universal runtime ordering, since joint solves may exploit shared factorizations or other within-group efficiencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coarser grouping offers fewer tasks and possible shared computation but larger critical tasks; finer grouping offers more parallelism at greater coordination overhead.
knowledge_statements.title: Grouping Granularity Tradeoffs

assumptions_latex: One coordination iteration solves every scenario subproblem once.
Scenario solve work is measured in a declared serial operation or oracle-call model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Serial scenario work is the sum of per-scenario work; with assigned parallel workers, ideal solve latency is the maximum worker load.

notation.meaning: work required to solve scenario s to the declared tolerance

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W_s(\varepsilon_s)\) denote the operations or oracle calls required to solve scenario \(s\) to its declared tolerance \(\varepsilon_s\). One complete serial scenario phase requires \[W_{\mathrm{serial}}=\sum_{s=1}^SW_s(\varepsilon_s).\] If scenarios are assigned disjointly to \(P\) workers, with worker \(w\) processing \(B_w\), the ideal synchronous solve-phase work on the critical path is \[W_{\mathrm{parallel}}=\max_{1\leq w\leq P}\sum_{s\in B_w}W_s(\varepsilon_s).\] Actual iteration cost additionally includes scheduling, communication, synchronization, and coordination work; the displayed quantity is therefore an ideal computational bound, not a wall-clock guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One iteration performs the sum of all scenario solve work serially; ideal parallel latency equals the largest assigned worker load, before overhead.

children.title: Scenario Memory Complexity
children.top_down_role: Storage scaling for scenario data, local states, and tree-indexed structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Memory Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak storage for explicit scenario copies and local solver states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let scenario \(s\) store a local state of dimension \(n_s\), a copied consensus vector of dimension \(m\), and \(O(1)\) auxiliary vectors of the same dimensions. An implementation retaining all \(S\) scenario states has peak memory \[M=\Theta\!\left(\sum_{s=1}^{S}n_s+Sm\right)\] scalar words. With \(P\) workers and a balanced assignment \(\mathcal S_p\), worker \(p\) stores \(\Theta(\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_p}n_s+|\mathcal S_p|m)\) words; replicated global metadata adds \(O(Pm)\) aggregate words.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit storage grows with all local scenario states and all copied consensus vectors; balanced distribution divides local storage among workers but may replicate global metadata.
assumptions_latex: \(S,P,m,n_s\in\mathbb N\).
Each retained scenario uses only a constant number of dense state vectors.
Scalar metadata per scenario is \(O(1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\Theta(\sum_s n_s+Sm)\).

notation.meaning: dimension of scenario s local state

children.title: Work–Storage Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Computational tradeoffs between retained data structures and repeated local work.

knowledge_statements.title: Work–Storage Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batching or checkpointing scenario states exchanges peak memory for recomputation under an explicit reconstruction model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each of \(S\) scenarios has state size \(d\), only \(b\) states are retained simultaneously, and reconstructing an evicted state costs \(C\ge 0\) units of work. Then peak scenario-state storage is \(M_b=\Theta(bd)\). If baseline work \(W_{\rm base}\) is independent of \(b\), the run performs \(R_b\) reconstructions, and \(R_b\) is nonincreasing in \(b\), then \(W_b=W_{\rm base}+R_bC\). Consequently, decreasing \(b\) reduces this storage linearly and cannot decrease work; full retention \(b=S\) has \(R_S=0\) when no other eviction occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated reconstruction model, retaining fewer scenario states reduces peak storage linearly but cannot decrease total work because evicted states must be reconstructed at nonnegative cost.
assumptions_latex: \(S,b,d\in\mathbb N\) with \(1\le b\le S\).
\(C\ge0\), and \(W_{\rm base}\) is independent of \(b\).
\(R_b\) is nonincreasing in \(b\), and \(R_S=0\) when full retention prevents eviction.
Reconstruction preserves the mathematical iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_b=\Theta(bd)\) and \(W_b=W_{\rm base}+R_bC\), so decreasing \(b\) cannot decrease \(W_b\).

notation.meaning: number of simultaneously retained scenario states
number of state reconstructions at batch size b

children.title: Scenario Communication Costs
children.top_down_role: Data-transfer costs arising from scenario aggregation and coordination.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Communication Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Word and message counts for synchronous star-coordinated scenario splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(K\) coordination rounds for \(S\) scenarios assigned in nonempty sets \(\mathcal S_1,\ldots,\mathcal S_P\) to \(P\le S\) workers. If every scenario sends one dense \(m\)-vector to a coordinator and receives one dense \(m\)-vector per round, the run communicates exactly \(2KSm\) scalar words in \(2KS\) logical scenario messages. If each worker instead packs all vectors for its assigned scenarios into one outgoing and one incoming message without changing their total dimension, the run still communicates \(2KSm\) words but uses \(2KP\) worker messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense scenario exchange communicates two m-vectors per scenario and round. Losslessly packing each worker's vectors preserves word volume while reducing the number of messages from two per scenario to two per worker.
assumptions_latex: \(K,S,P,m\in\mathbb N\) with \(P\le S\).
The nonempty sets \(\mathcal S_1,\ldots,\mathcal S_P\) partition the \(S\) scenarios.
Communication uses a star coordinator, and every scenario participates in every round.
Worker packing changes message boundaries but not the total transmitted vector dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unaggregated cost is \(2KSm\) words and \(2KS\) messages; lossless worker packing gives \(2KSm\) words and \(2KP\) messages.

notation.meaning: dimension of each communicated scenario vector

children.title: Scenario Synchronization Costs
children.top_down_role: Barrier and waiting costs arising from coordinated scenario updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Synchronization Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier latency in a synchronous coordination model with concurrently measured scenario phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each round \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), let \(t_{s,k}\ge0\) be the elapsed completion time, measured from the common phase start, of scenario \(s\in\{1,\ldots,S\}\), and let \(\ell_k\ge0\) be subsequent barrier and coordination latency. If the next round cannot begin until every scenario completes, then \[T_{\rm sync}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\max_{1\le s\le S}t_{s,k}+\ell_k\right).\] Thus the slowest scenario completion determines each computation phase, and the \(K\) barriers contribute total latency \(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\ell_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When scenario completion times are measured from a common phase start, each synchronous round lasts until the slowest scenario completes and then incurs its barrier latency.
assumptions_latex: \(K,S\in\mathbb N\).
For every \(s,k\), \(t_{s,k}\ge0\) is a phase-completion time measured from the common start of round \(k\).
Every scenario must complete before round \(k+1\) begins.
Communication not represented by \(\ell_k\) is included in \(t_{s,k}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\rm sync}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\max_{1\le s\le S}t_{s,k}+\ell_k)\).

notation.meaning: elapsed completion time of scenario s in round k

children.title: Communication-Avoiding Regimes
children.top_down_role: Execution regimes that reduce coordination traffic through locality or aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Avoiding Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination cost when several local stages are performed per exchange under a fixed-accuracy performance model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose both a baseline method and a grouped method attain the same prescribed accuracy after \(K\) local update stages. The baseline exchanges one block of \(Sm\) scalar words after every stage. If the grouped method performs \(q\ge1\) stages between exchanges, it uses \(R_q=\lceil K/q\rceil\) communication rounds and transmits \(V_q=R_qSm\) scalar words. Under the round-cost model \(L+Sm/B\), if grouping adds \(A_q\ge0\) units of local runtime, then grouping improves modeled runtime exactly when \[A_q<(K-R_q)(L+Sm/B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed accuracy and a fixed number of local stages, communicating once every q stages reduces the number of exchanges to the ceiling of K divided by q. It helps when the saved latency and bandwidth time exceed the added local runtime.
assumptions_latex: \(K,S,m,q\in\mathbb N\) with \(q\ge1\).
The baseline and grouped methods attain the same prescribed accuracy after \(K\) local stages.
Each exchange transmits exactly \(Sm\) scalar words.
\(B>0\), \(L\ge0\), and the additional local runtime satisfies \(A_q\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_q=\lceil K/q\rceil\), \(V_q=R_qSm\), and grouping improves the modeled runtime iff \(A_q<(K-R_q)(L+Sm/B)\).

notation.meaning: local update stages per communication round
additional local runtime caused by grouping

children.title: Scenario Explosion
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial growth of scenario paths, duplicated variables, and coupling relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial growth in an explicitly enumerated multistage scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a depth-\(T\) scenario tree in which every node at stage \(t-1\) has \(b_t\) children, the number of complete paths is \(N_T=\prod_{t=1}^{T}b_t\), and the number of tree nodes is \(1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\prod_{j=1}^{t}b_j\). If every path receives an independent copy of a \(d\)-dimensional decision vector before nonanticipativity is imposed, pathwise storage and the number of copied decision coordinates are \(\Theta(dN_T)\). Constant branching \(b_t=b>1\) therefore produces exponential growth \(\Theta(b^T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit enumeration multiplies branching factors across stages; pathwise variable copies and their storage consequently grow exponentially under constant branching.
assumptions_latex: \(T,d,b_t\in\mathbb N\).
All branches and complete paths are explicitly retained.
Each complete path has a decision copy of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_T=\prod_t b_t\), and for \(b_t=b>1\), pathwise storage is \(\Theta(db^T)\).

children.title: Weak Scenario Separability
children.top_down_role: Dense cross-scenario structure leaving little useful independent computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Scenario Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense coupling eliminates most independent scenario computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the coupling graph have one vertex per scenario and an edge whenever two scenario blocks occur together in a constraint or objective term. If this graph is complete and evaluating every cross-scenario term costs at least one operation, then a full coupled evaluation requires \(\Omega(S^2)\) work. Scenario-wise parallelization can distribute local terms, but it cannot reduce these dense coupling evaluations to \(O(S)\) work without additional algebraic structure, approximation, or sparsification. Thus nominal scenario blocks alone do not imply useful separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every scenario directly couples to every other, evaluating coupling terms is quadratic, so scenario labels alone provide little independent computation.
assumptions_latex: There are \(S\) scenario blocks.
Every unordered scenario pair contributes a nonzero coupling term.
No shared low-rank, aggregate, or sparsified representation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense pairwise coupling entails \(\Omega(S^2)\) coupling work per full evaluation.

children.title: Nonconvex Duality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes where dual coordination does not recover primal solution quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dual coordination when strong duality is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonconvex problem \(p^\star=\inf\{f(x):g(x)=0,\ x\in X\}\), define the Lagrangian dual value \(d^\star=\sup_{\lambda}\inf_{x\in X}[f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)\rangle]\). Weak duality gives \(d^\star\le p^\star\), but nonconvexity does not ensure equality. When \(\Delta=p^\star-d^\star>0\), optimizing coordination multipliers can approach at most \(d^\star\); it cannot by itself certify or recover a primal solution of value below \(d^\star+\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive nonconvex duality gap makes the best multiplier bound strictly weaker than the primal optimum, limiting dual-only coordination and certification.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and may be nonconvex or discrete.
\(p^\star\) and \(d^\star\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta=p^\star-d^\star>0\) implies dual optimization alone does not close the primal optimality gap.

children.title: Integer Disagreement Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Persistent disagreement among scenario-local discrete decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Disagreement Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent consensus residuals caused by cycling discrete scenario decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let scenario decisions satisfy \(x_s^k\in X_s\subset\mathbb Z^m\), and define the consensus residual \(r^k=\max_s\|x_s^k-\bar x^k\|\). If a deterministic coordination update enters a cycle of period \(q\ge1\), so \(x_s^{k+q}=x_s^k\) for every \(s\), and every point in that cycle has \(r^k\ge\delta>0\), then no later iterate satisfies a consensus stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon<\delta\). Bounded objectives or multiplier changes do not remove this residual-based stagnation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once discrete scenario decisions cycle while remaining separated by at least delta, a tighter consensus tolerance can never be reached.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_s\) is discrete.
The coordination update is deterministic on its full state.
The iterate cycle has residual lower bound \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^k\ge\delta>\varepsilon\) for all iterates after entry into the cycle.

notation.meaning: scenario s integer decision at iteration k

children.title: Gap-Induced Recovery Failure
children.top_down_role: Policy-recovery limitations associated with unresolved duality gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Induced Recovery Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of primal recovery from a dual bound separated by a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d^\star<p^\star\) be finite dual and primal optimal values with \(\Delta=p^\star-d^\star>0\). For any recovered primal-feasible point \(\hat x\), weak duality yields \(f(\hat x)-d^\star\ge\Delta\). Hence a recovery procedure whose success certificate requires \(f(\hat x)-d^\star\le\varepsilon\) must fail whenever \(\varepsilon<\Delta\), even if it recovers a primal optimizer. The failure concerns certification relative to the dual bound, not necessarily primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the duality gap exceeds the requested tolerance, no feasible recovered point—even an optimizer—can satisfy a dual-bound recovery certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(d^\star<p^\star\) are finite.
Recovery outputs a primal-feasible \(\hat x\).
Success is tested by \(f(\hat x)-d^\star\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon<\Delta\) implies the stated recovery certificate is impossible.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Scenario Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear convergence slowdown for a quadratic coordination model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the coordination objective be \(\phi(z)=\tfrac12 z^\top Hz-h^\top z\), where \(H\) is symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues in \([\mu,L]\). Gradient coordination with the optimal constant step \(\alpha=2/(L+\mu)\) satisfies \[\|z^{k+1}-z^\star\|_2\le\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\|z^k-z^\star\|_2,\qquad \kappa=L/\mu.\] Therefore heterogeneous scaling or weak agreement curvature that makes \(\kappa\) large drives the contraction factor toward one and increases coordination iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic coordination, a large condition number makes the best fixed-step gradient contraction approach one, causing slow agreement.
assumptions_latex: \(H=H^\top\succ0\).
\(0<\mu\le\lambda_{\min}(H)\le\lambda_{\max}(H)\le L\).
A constant step \(2/(L+\mu)\) is used.

children.title: Scenario Stragglers
children.top_down_role: Individual scenario subproblems whose runtimes delay coordinated progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Stragglers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idle-time penalty from slow scenarios under barrier synchronization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In synchronous round \(k\), let worker \(p\) require time \(T_{p,k}\) for its assigned scenarios. The computation phase lasts \(M_k=\max_pT_{p,k}\), and aggregate worker idle time is \[I_k=\sum_{p=1}^{P}(M_k-T_{p,k})=PM_k-\sum_{p=1}^{P}T_{p,k}.\] Thus one straggling worker with time \(M_k\) delays every faster worker until the barrier. Across \(K\) rounds, straggler-induced idle time is \(\sum_k I_k\), excluding communication latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each barrier, the slowest worker sets round duration; the difference between that duration and each worker's time is accumulated idle work.
assumptions_latex: All \(P\) workers must finish before round \(k+1\).
Worker times \(T_{p,k}\ge0\) include assigned scenario computation.
Communication latency is accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_k=P\max_pT_{p,k}-\sum_pT_{p,k}\).

children.title: Scenario Load Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Uneven distribution of scenario work across computational resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Load Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous scenario decomposition with static assignment and heterogeneous scenario costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let worker \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) receive scenarios \(P_j\), where the sets \(P_j\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), and let scenario \(s\) require time \(\tau_s\geq0\). Define \(L_j=\sum_{s\in P_j}\tau_s\), \(T=\max_j L_j\), and \(\bar L=m^{-1}\sum_jL_j\). With a barrier after every local solve and negligible communication, the parallel efficiency relative to perfectly balanced execution is at most \(\bar L/T\). Thus the imbalance ratio \(R=T/\bar L\) imposes efficiency at most \(1/R\); any family with \(R\to\infty\) has vanishing parallel efficiency despite increasing worker count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static assignments whose maximum worker load greatly exceeds the average force synchronous parallel efficiency toward zero.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) form a disjoint partition of the scenarios.
Scenario processing times \(\tau_s\) are nonnegative and additive within each worker.
Each iteration ends with a global barrier, with communication time neglected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\leq \bar L/T=1/R\), so \(R\to\infty\) implies \(E\to0\).

notation.meaning: total scenario-processing load assigned to worker j

children.title: Barrier Amplification
children.top_down_role: Synchronization losses caused by heterogeneous scenario completion times.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact idle-time amplification at a synchronous scenario-solver barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For worker loads \(L_1,\ldots,L_m\), let the barrier release at \(T=\max_jL_j\). The aggregate idle time accumulated before release is \(I=\sum_{j=1}^m(T-L_j)=mT-\sum_jL_j\). Suppose worker \(q\) is uniquely critical and its load increases by \(\delta>0\) while all other loads remain below \(L_q+\delta\). Then the new release time is \(T+\delta\), worker \(q\) contributes no additional idleness, and every other worker waits an additional \(\delta\). Consequently, elapsed time grows by \(\delta\) while aggregate idle time grows by \((m-1)\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical worker’s delay is replicated as waiting on every other worker, multiplying aggregate idle time by the worker count minus one.
assumptions_latex: All workers synchronize at one blocking barrier.
Worker \(q\) remains the unique critical worker after its load increases by \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T'=T+\delta\) and \(I'-I=(m-1)\delta\).

notation.meaning: work time of worker j before the barrier

children.title: Dual Ascent Lineage
children.top_down_role: Historical development of multiplier-based price coordination through dual ascent.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Ascent Lineage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical dual-gradient or dual-supergradient ascent for a finite-dimensional equality-constrained convex program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\). For \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), choose \(y^0\in\mathbb R^q\) and steps \(\alpha_k>0\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x)+\langle y^k,Ax-b\rangle\}\) and set \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\alpha_k(Ax^{k+1}-b)\). For the concave dual function \(d(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\}\), the residual \(Ax^{k+1}-b\) is a supergradient of \(d\) at \(y^k\). If \(d\) is differentiable there, then \(Ax^{k+1}-b=\nabla d(y^k)\), so the multiplier update is dual-gradient ascent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual ascent alternates Lagrangian minimization with a multiplier step along a dual supergradient given by the equality-constraint residual; it is gradient ascent where the dual function is differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The Lagrangian infimum is attained at every generated multiplier.
The selected steps make the multiplier updates well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\alpha_k(Ax^{k+1}-b)\), where \(Ax^{k+1}-b\in\partial^+d(y^k)\), and it equals \(\nabla d(y^k)\) whenever \(d\) is differentiable at \(y^k\).

notation.meaning: concave superdifferential of the dual function

children.title: Dual Decomposition Lineage
children.top_down_role: Historical development of separable subproblem coordination through dual decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Decomposition Lineage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable Lagrangian representation induced by a finite-dimensional coupling constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\in\mathbb N\), let \(X_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_s}\), let \(f_s:\mathbb R^{n_s}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(A_s\in\mathbb R^{q\times n_s}\), and let \(b\in\mathbb R^q\). Consider \(\min_{x_s\in X_s}\sum_{s=1}^N f_s(x_s)\) subject to \(\sum_{s=1}^N A_sx_s=b\). For \(y\in\mathbb R^q\), the Lagrangian separates as \(L(x,y)=\sum_{s=1}^N(f_s(x_s)+\langle y,A_sx_s\rangle)-\langle y,b\rangle\). Hence \(d(y)=\sum_{s=1}^N d_s(y)-\langle y,b\rangle\), where \(d_s(y)=\inf_{x_s\in X_s}(f_s(x_s)+\langle y,A_sx_s\rangle)\). The local infima can therefore be computed independently for a fixed shared multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the shared coupling equality converts the separable primal program into independent block infima coordinated by one multiplier.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_s\) is a nonempty convex subset of \(\mathbb R^{n_s}\).
Each \(f_s\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The displayed local Lagrangian infima are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(y)=\sum_{s=1}^N d_s(y)-\langle y,b\rangle\), with each \(d_s(y)\) independently evaluable for fixed \(y\).

notation.meaning: primal variable of block or scenario s
multiplier for the shared coupling constraint
local dual contribution of block s

children.title: Price-Coordination Transition
children.top_down_role: Conceptual transition from dual price updates to augmented alternating coordination.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Coordination Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretation of dual multipliers as coordinating prices for finite-dimensional decomposed blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(N\in\mathbb N\), let \(X_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_s}\), \(f_s:\mathbb R^{n_s}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(A_s\in\mathbb R^{q\times n_s}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\). In the problem \(\min_{x_s\in X_s}\sum_{s=1}^N f_s(x_s)\) subject to \(\sum_{s=1}^N A_sx_s=b\), announce a price \(y^k\in\mathbb R^q\) and let each block choose \(x_s^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_s\in X_s}\{f_s(x_s)+\langle y^k,A_sx_s\rangle\}\). Define \(r^{k+1}=\sum_{s=1}^N A_sx_s^{k+1}-b\) and update \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\alpha_kr^{k+1}\), where \(\alpha_k>0\). Thus the primal responses remain local while the common price is adjusted from the aggregate coupling imbalance; this is dual ascent applied to the dual-decomposition representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual decomposition becomes price coordination when one multiplier is broadcast as a price and updated from the aggregate resource imbalance.
assumptions_latex: Each local price-response minimization is attained.
The residual sign convention is \(\sum_{s=1}^N A_sx_s-b\).
The multiplier steps satisfy \(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\alpha_k\bigl(\sum_{s=1}^N A_sx_s^{k+1}-b\bigr)\) coordinates the otherwise independent block responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Method-of-Multipliers Lineage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint augmented-Lagrangian minimization preceding ADMM's alternating block updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(g:\mathbb R^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^q\). For \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,z\in\mathbb R^p}f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), choose \(\rho>0\), initialize \(y^0\in\mathbb R^q\), and define \(L_\rho(x,z,y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz-c\rVert^2\). The method of multipliers computes \((x^{k+1},z^{k+1})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x,z}L_\rho(x,z,y^k)\) jointly and then sets \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\). ADMM descends from this scheme by replacing the joint primal minimization with successive minimizations over the two blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method of multipliers jointly minimizes an augmented Lagrangian, whereas ADMM replaces that joint solve with alternating block solves.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The affine equality is feasible.
Every generated joint augmented-Lagrangian subproblem attains a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal variables jointly minimize \(L_\rho\), after which \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\).

children.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Duality
children.top_down_role: The operator-splitting correspondence linking dual ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford–ADMM Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus-form equivalence between primal ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting on the dual inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be proper, closed, convex functions on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and consider \(\min_{x,z}f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(x-z=0\). Its dual is \(\min_y f^*(-y)+g^*(y)\), whose optimality inclusion is \(0\in\partial(f^*\circ(-I))(y)+\partial g^*(y)\). For any \(\rho>0\), standard two-block ADMM on the primal is equivalent, under a fixed affine identification of initialized auxiliary and multiplier variables, to Douglas–Rachford splitting with stepsize \(\rho\) on these two dual subdifferentials. Corresponding resolvent shadows recover the ADMM block solutions and multiplier sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For consensus problems, primal ADMM is Douglas–Rachford splitting applied to the sum of the two dual subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
A primal-dual solution exists.
The ADMM and Douglas–Rachford states use corresponding initializations and the same positive stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal ADMM and dual Douglas–Rachford splitting generate corresponding iterates under an affine state transformation.

children.title: Proximal-Point Interpretation of ADMM

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Point Interpretation of ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: ADMM represented as proximal-point iteration on an operator induced by dual Douglas–Rachford splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone operators arising from the dual optimality inclusion associated with ADMM. For \(\gamma>0\), define \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\), \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I\), and analogously \(J_{\gamma B}\) and \(R_{\gamma B}\). Under the ADMM–Douglas–Rachford state identification, set \(S=\frac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\); then \(w^{k+1}=S(w^k)\) for \(w^k\in\mathcal H\). Since \(S\) is firmly nonexpansive, the set-valued operator \(M=S^{-1}-I\) is maximal monotone and \(S=(I+M)^{-1}\). Hence the state corresponding to ADMM satisfies the proximal-point iteration \(w^{k+1}=(I+M)^{-1}w^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Through its Douglas–Rachford dual state, ADMM is a proximal-point iteration for a derived maximal monotone operator.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximal monotone operators on the real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).
\(\gamma>0\), and the ADMM state is identified with the corresponding Douglas–Rachford state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^{k+1}=(I+M)^{-1}w^k\) for the maximal monotone operator \(M=S^{-1}-I\).

children.title: Canonical Two-Block Interface
children.top_down_role: The standard separable two-block coupling structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Two-Block Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional two-block separable equality-constrained form used by ADMM.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical two-block ADMM interface is the optimization problem \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\,z\in\mathbb R^p}\ f(x)+g(z)\qquad\operatorname{subject\ to}\qquad Ax+Bz=c,\] where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb R^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, convex functions, \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^q\). The objective is separable across the two primal blocks; all interaction occurs through the affine equality, which supplies the residual used by ADMM's multiplier update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical ADMM problem has two separable convex objective blocks coupled only by one affine equality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The affine constraint \(Ax+Bz=c\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem has separable objective \(f(x)+g(z)\) and coupling residual \(Ax+Bz-c\).

children.title: Graph-Form Representations
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable representations organized around graph-form objective components.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Form Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-form encoding of a linear composition as a two-block equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) be linear and let \(f\) and \(g\) be extended-real-valued functions on \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathbb R^p\), respectively. The composite problem \(\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)\) has the graph-form representation \[\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad (x,z)\in\operatorname{gra}K,\] equivalently \(Kx-z=0\), where \(\operatorname{gra}K=\{(x,z):z=Kx\}\). Feasible points correspond bijectively through \(z=Kx\), and corresponding points have identical objective values; therefore both formulations have the same optimal value and mapped minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear composition becomes a two-block problem by constraining the auxiliary variable to lie on the graph of the linear map.
assumptions_latex: \(K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear.
The composite objective is proper at some point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x[f(x)+g(Kx)]=\min_{Kx-z=0}[f(x)+g(z)]\), with minimizers related by \(z=Kx\).

children.title: Constraint Splitting
children.top_down_role: Decompositions that separate constraint components through auxiliary structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator-function splitting of multiple convex constraints through replicated variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\dots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The constrained problem \(\min_{x\in\cap_{i=1}^m C_i}f(x)\) is equivalently \[\min_{x,z_1,\dots,z_m}\ f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{C_i}(z_i)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad z_i=x\quad(i=1,\dots,m),\] where \(\delta_{C_i}(z)=0\) for \(z\in C_i\) and \(\delta_{C_i}(z)=+\infty\) otherwise. The consensus equalities isolate every constraint in its own block while preserving feasible points, objective values, and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicated variables and indicator functions isolate each convex constraint while consensus equalities preserve the original feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The split formulation is equivalent to minimizing \(f\) over \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).

notation.meaning: indicator function of constraint set i
consensus constraint linking each replica to x

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces connecting duplicated variables, simple components, and coupling constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General variable-lifting interface that exposes separable terms to two-block splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(K_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{p_i}\) be linear, let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(g_i:\mathbb R^{p_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for \(i=1,\dots,m\). Introducing \(z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\), the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(K_ix)\) has the representation \[\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(z_i)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad K_ix-z_i=0\quad(i=1,\dots,m).\] Projection onto \(x\) gives a bijection between feasible lifted points and original points because every feasible auxiliary block satisfies \(z_i=K_ix\). Objective values and minimizers are preserved, while the lifted objective is separable in the auxiliary blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables lift several compositions into separate objective blocks connected to the original variable by linear equalities.
assumptions_latex: Every \(K_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{p_i}\) is linear.
The original composite objective is proper at some point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted and original problems have equal optimal values, with \(z_i=K_ix\) at every feasible lifted point.

notation.meaning: separable function applied to auxiliary block i

children.title: Primal Partition Choices
children.top_down_role: Block decompositions organized around primal variables or primal constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(m,q,n_1,\ldots,n_m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(f_j:\mathbb{R}^{n_j}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(M_j:\mathbb{R}^{n_j}\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear for \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
\(d\in\mathbb{R}^q\), and the constraint \(\sum_{j=1}^m M_jw_j=d\) is feasible.
\(I\) and \(J\) are nonempty disjoint sets satisfying \(I\cup J=\{1,ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reformulation \(\min_{u,v}\{f(u)+g(v):Au+Bv=d\}\) is equivalent to the original problem, and its computational suitability depends on the resulting block-solution interfaces.

notation.meaning: Stacked variables indexed by the two parts
Separable objectives associated with the two parts
Linear block operators assembled from the original constraint maps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex two-block partitions used to expose an ADMM interface.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the separable linearly constrained problem \[\min_{w_1,\ldots,w_m}\ \sum_{j=1}^m f_j(w_j)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j=1}^m M_jw_j=d,\] a bipartition \(I\mathbin{\dot\cup}J=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) induces the equivalent two-block representation \[\min_{u,v}\ f(u)+g(v)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Au+Bv=d.\] The partition supplies a usable ADMM interface when each resulting augmented block minimization is well-defined and evaluable by the intended local proximal, projection, or structured linear-system solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grouping the primal variables and objective terms into two nonempty blocks gives an equivalent two-block ADMM representation; its computational suitability depends on whether both augmented block subproblems admit the intended local solution interfaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Partition Choices

children.title: Dual Partition Choices
children.top_down_role: Block decompositions organized around dual variables or dual coupling structure.

assumptions_latex: \(n_u,n_v,q\in\mathbb{N}\), \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n_u}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^{n_v}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(A:\mathbb{R}^{n_u}\to\mathbb{R}^q\) and \(B:\mathbb{R}^{n_v}\to\mathbb{R}^q\) are linear, and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^q\).
The primal problem \(\inf\{f(u)+g(v):Au+Bv=d\}\) satisfies a qualification ensuring strong Fenchel duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate-form dual minimization has objective \(\Phi(y)=f^*(-A^{\mathsf T}y)+g^*(-B^{\mathsf T}y)+\langle d,y\rangle\), with \(\inf_y\Phi(y)=-p^*\) under strong duality.

notation.meaning: Multiplier in the primal constraint space
Fenchel conjugates of the two block objectives
Optimal value of the primal minimization
Objective of the conjugate-form dual minimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel dual partition induced by a finite-dimensional two-block primal formulation.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p^*=\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{n_u},\,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n_v}}\ f(u)+g(v)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Au+Bv=d,\] minimizing the Lagrangian over \(u\) and \(v\) yields the dual maximization with objective \(-\Phi(y)\), or equivalently the conjugate-form dual minimization \[\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^q}\ \Phi(y)=f^*(-A^{\mathsf T}y)+g^*(-B^{\mathsf T}y)+\langle d,y\rangle.\] Under strong duality, \(\inf_y\Phi(y)=-p^*\). A dual partition assigns the conjugate terms, affine term, and any introduced multiplier copies to blocks while imposing equality constraints between copies representing the same multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualization replaces the primal block objectives by conjugates composed with adjoint operators. In the conjugate minimization convention its optimal value is the negative of the primal value, and copied multipliers must agree across partition blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Partition Choices

children.title: Partition Dualization Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural tradeoffs governing whether coupling is partitioned before or after dualization.

assumptions_latex: A finite-dimensional convex primal problem and its Lagrange dual satisfy strong duality.
Each primal or dual partition under comparison is an exact reformulation of its corresponding optimization problem.
The compared block subproblems are solved exactly or according to a specified controlled-inexactness rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact primal and dual partitions preserve their respective optimal values; the dual maximization value equals the primal value, whereas the conjugate-form dual minimization value is its negative, and computational costs remain partition-dependent.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the primal minimization
Optimal value of the Lagrange-dual maximization
Optimal value of the equivalent conjugate-form dual minimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural comparison of exact primal and dual partitions, without asserting a universal convergence or cost ordering.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under strong duality, the primal minimization value and Lagrange-dual maximization value satisfy \(p^*=d^*\). If the dual is instead written as the conjugate-form minimization obtained by negating the dual objective, then \(\phi^*=-p^*\). Exact repartitioning does not alter the relevant primal or dual optimization problem, but it can change the block subproblems, communicated quantities, available parallelism, and numerical conditioning. These costs depend on the particular operators, dimensions, and solver implementation, so convexity alone gives no universal ordering between primal and dual partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong duality equates the primal value with the dual maximization value, while the conjugate dual minimization has the opposite value. Exact partitions preserve these values but can have different local solves, communication costs, parallelism, and conditioning, with no universal ordering from convexity alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Partition Dualization Tradeoffs

children.title: Subproblem Proximal Structure
children.top_down_role: Local proximal, projection, linear-system, or structured-solver interfaces inherited by the blocks.

assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is linear, \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\) is symmetric positive definite, \(q\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(\rho>0\).
The displayed block subproblem has at least one minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity-map case is a metric proximal problem; indicators then yield metric projections, while convex quadratic objectives yield a linear system that is uniquely solvable when its coefficient matrix is positive definite.

notation.meaning: Squared norm induced by the positive-definite metric
Indicator function of a nonempty closed convex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local solution interfaces for finite-dimensional convex ADMM block updates.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ADMM block subproblem with local objective \(h\), linear map \(L\), residual target \(q\), penalty \(\rho\), and metric \(P\) has the form \[x^+\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{h(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Lx-q\|_P^2\right\}.\] When \(L=I_n\), this is \(x^+\in\operatorname{prox}^{P}_{h/\rho}(q)\); if additionally \(h=\delta_C\) for a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), it is the metric projection of \(q\) onto \(C\). If \(h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Hx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle\) with \(H\) symmetric positive semidefinite, every minimizer satisfies \[(H+\rho L^{\mathsf T}PL)x=\rho L^{\mathsf T}Pq-a.\] This system has a unique solution when \(H+\rho L^{\mathsf T}PL\) is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ADMM block is a metric proximal evaluation when its linear map is the identity; indicators then give metric projections. Convex quadratic blocks satisfy a structured linear system, with uniqueness when the system matrix is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.title: Subproblem Proximal Structure

children.title: Global-Variable Consensus
children.top_down_role: Local objective copies coordinated through a shared global variable.

assumptions_latex: \(N,n\in\mathbb{N}\), and \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,N\).
The common-variable problem \(\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(z)\) has a solution.

notation.meaning: Local copy owned by agent or scenario i

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The common-variable problem \[\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \sum_{i=1}^N f_i(z)\] has the equivalent global-variable consensus representation \[\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_N,z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i=z\quad(i=1,\ldots,N).\] The constraints separate the local objective evaluations while the global variable \(z\) coordinates agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common-variable sum is equivalently represented by assigning each objective a local copy and constraining every copy to equal one global coordinating variable.

children.title: General-Form Consensus
children.top_down_role: Agreement among heterogeneous local representations or mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(N,p,n_1,\ldots,n_N,q_1,\ldots,q_N\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(f_i:\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for \(i=1,\ldots,N\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(A_i:\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\to\mathbb{R}^{q_i}\) and \(B_i:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^{q_i}\) are linear for \(i=1,\ldots,N\), and the system \(A_ix_i=B_iz\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equations \(A_ix_i=B_iz\) impose agreement between heterogeneous local representations and the corresponding representations of a shared latent variable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-image consensus allowing different finite-dimensional local spaces and representations.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general-form consensus problem is \[\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_N,z}\ \sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_i)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad A_ix_i=B_iz\quad(i=1,\ldots,N).\] Consensus is imposed on the represented quantities rather than requiring the heterogeneous variables \(x_i\) themselves to coincide. Global-variable consensus is the special case \(n_i=p=q_i\), \(A_i=I_p\), \(B_i=I_p\), and \(g=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General-form consensus equates linear representations of heterogeneous local variables with corresponding representations of a shared latent variable; ordinary global-variable consensus is the identity-map special case.
knowledge_statements.title: General-Form Consensus

children.title: Graph-Consensus Formulations
children.top_down_role: Neighbor agreement organized by vertices and edges of a communication graph.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected graph, and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).
For every \(i\in V\), \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The graph-consensus optimization problem has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For connected \(G\), the edge constraints \(x_i=x_j\) are equivalent to the existence of one \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(x_i=z\) for every \(i\in V\).

notation.meaning: Communication graph with vertex and edge sets
Vertex-by-edge incidence matrix after assigning an arbitrary edge orientation
Vector obtained by stacking the local decisions in a fixed vertex order

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected finite undirected graph consensus with equality constraints on communication edges.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Graph consensus represents distributed optimization as \[\min_{(x_i)_{i\in V}}\ \sum_{i\in V}f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i=x_j\quad\text{for every }\{i,j\}\in E.\] After assigning an arbitrary orientation to the edges and forming the vertex-by-edge incidence matrix \(D\), the constraints are equivalently \[(D^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)x=0.\] Because \(G\) is connected, this condition is equivalent to \(x=\mathbf{1}_{|V|}\otimes z\) for some \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), so only neighbor equalities are required to impose global agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local variables agree across communication edges. On a connected graph these neighbor equalities are equivalent to one global consensus value and can be written using the graph incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Consensus Formulations

children.title: Factor-Graph Consensus
children.top_down_role: Consensus organized by variable-factor incidence and overlapping local scopes.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(V\) are finite factor and variable index sets with incidence relation \(E\subseteq F\times V\).
Each factor objective \(f_a\) is proper, closed, convex on the product of spaces in its scope.
Every local copy and its corresponding global variable have the same Euclidean dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Incidence constraints \(x_{aj}=z_j\) make overlapping factor scopes consistent without duplicating objective coupling.

notation.meaning: Local copy of variable j used by factor a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus over overlapping factor scopes in a bipartite incidence graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each factor \(a\in F\), let \(N(a)=\{j\in V:(a,j)\in E\}\) and introduce the local scope \(x_a=(x_{aj})_{j\in N(a)}\). Factor-graph consensus has the form \[\min_{(x_a),(z_j)}\ \sum_{a\in F}f_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_{aj}=z_j\quad((a,j)\in E).\] Thus each factor evaluates its objective using local copies, while all factors incident to the same variable index agree through \(z_j\). Eliminating the copies recovers the objective over consistent overlapping scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each factor owns copies of variables in its scope, and incidence equalities tie all copies of the same variable to one representative.
knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Graph Consensus

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factor-incidence copy representation is mathematically coherent and representation is the correct content kind, but no inspectable citation or exact locator is supplied. Standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for this review layer.
